newsitem.title: UNITED NATIONS: US proposes lowering UN dues, angering Europeans.
newsitem.headline: US proposes lowering UN dues, angering Europeans.

text.p: The United States formally asked a high-level U.N. committee on Monday to lower its dues from 25 to 20 percent, a proposal scoffed at by Europeans as long as Washington owed the world body over $1 billion.

Jan Berteling, the deputy envoy of the Netherlands. said the European Union would only consider the U.S. proposals if there was some committement to pay off the huge arrears that were crippling the world body.
"The EU will consider the U.S. proposals carefully," he said. But it needed "a firm commitment to meet assessed contributions in full and on time and without conditions."
"The United States has not a positive record regarding implementing previous agreements to pay U.S. arrears," he said suggesting that there should be penalities for late payment.

The committee, made up of ambassadors or their deputies, has been considering an EU proposals to revamp U.N. dues and peacekeeping contributions, which would somewhat lower Washington's obligation but not nearly as much as the U.S. Congress insist it wants.
Washington a year ago said it would propose a 20 percent ceiling for its dues and did so formally on Monday.

U.S. Ambassador Bill Richardson said that U.S. President Bill Clinton had "made repaying our debt to the United Nations a foreign policy priority." But he warned that Washington would not allow "our multi-faceted relationship with the U.N. to be defined by the single issue of our arrearages."
U.S. envoy Victor Marrero outlined Washington's proposals on financial payments that left the Europeans paying even more than they would under increases they had already accepted.

In a veiled reference to CHina, he also insisted that no permanent member of the Security Council should get any kind of a discount because its gross national product was low, a proposal many diplomats privately welcomed. China so far has not agreed to substantial increases.

Marrero as a whole approved the EU proposals that are based on gross national product with various discounts for poor nations and frequent revisions as a country's economy changes. But he said there had to be a ceiling of 20 percent of what any one member paid for dues and 25 percent for peacekeeping contributions.

Currently, there is a ceiling of 25 percent for dues negotiated previously by the United States, which has more than 27 percent of the world's wealth. The five permanent members of the Security Council also pay a surcharge for peacekeeping.
Congress last year unilaterally lowered the U.S. contribution from 30 to 25 percent for peacekeeping.
President Clinton has promised to pay the U.N. debt by 1999, albeit a lower amount than the U.N. says it is owed.
But conservatives in Congress are far from approving any contributions unless the world body severely streamlines its bureaucracy first and abolishes many of its programmes.
